item.title: Sebi orders Avadhut Sathe Trading Academy and its founder to refund ₹546 cr
item.description: The regulator has also barred the academy and Sathe from accessing the securities market for two years or until compliance with the refund direction, whichever is later ...
item.dc:creator: Press Trust of India
item.content:encoded: Markets regulator Sebi on Friday directed Avadhut Sathe Trading Academy Pvt Ltd (ASTAPL) and its Founder Avadhut Sathe to refund Rs 546.17 crore collected from participants for providing unregistered investment advisory and research analyst services, along with interest of Rs 67.87 crore.The regulator has also barred the academy and Sathe from accessing the securities market for two years or until compliance with the refund direction, whichever is later.In its 171-page final order, the regulator imposed a total penalty of Rs 11.5 crore on the academy, Sathe and Gouri Avadhut Sathe for violations of securities market regulations.The academy has been fined Rs 6 crore, Sathe has been fined Rs 4 crore, while Gouri Avadhut Sathe has been penalised Rs 1.5 crore.The regulator found that the academy and Sathe provided investment advice and research recommendations through paid programmes, sessions and WhatsApp groups without obtaining the required registration.It also found that misleading promotional representations about returns were used to attract participants and that investment advice was provided without assessing the suitability of recommendations for recipients.The order said the academy and Sathe had collected around Rs 601.38 crore from course participants since inception. However, based on the evidence examined, fees of Rs 546.17 crore attributable to the relevant programmes were identified for disgorgement and refund.Sebi has directed the academy and Sathe to complete the refunds within five months of receiving the order. They have also been asked to publish notices in newspapers within 30 days, explaining the procedure for investors to claim refunds.The regulator has further directed that their bank accounts remain frozen for debits until the required amounts are deposited into the designated account and Sebi's Investor Protection and Education Fund, as applicable.Gouri Avadhut Sathe has been barred from accessing the securities market for six months. Sebi said her liability arose from a failure to exercise oversight.

item.title: 'Political leadership' clear on theatre commands, says defence secretary
item.description: In an era where warfare involves multiples domains such as space, cyber, land, sea and air, the integrated theatre commands are needed to safeguard India's interests, Rajesh Kumar Singh said ...
item.dc:creator: Satarupa Bhattacharjya
item.content:encoded: The government is keen to integrate the country’s armed forces into theatre commands, Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh said on Friday. “The political leadership is very clear that we have to move towards the integration of the three services into theatre commands,” so that national power can be applied in a strategic manner, Singh said at a seminar organised by accounting firm KPMG in New Delhi.  “That process is underway. A blueprint has been prepared, and we are awaiting approval at the highest level.” In an era where warfare involves multiple domains such as space, cyber, land, sea and air, the integrated theatre commands are needed to safeguard India’s interests, Singh said. “We are moving in that direction.” While the idea of the integrated theatre commands has been doing the rounds of discussions since the Kargil War of 1999, the armed forces have submitted a proposal to the government in recent months. The Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS), which is the clearing authority, has yet to approve the proposal.  Former Chief of Defence Staff General (CDS) Anil Chauhan (retired) had told Business Standard earlier while still in office that the proposed structure would include both land and sea-based theatre commands, reflecting India’s strategic challenges and opportunities. Although approved by the CCS in 2019, the CDS post was an aftereffect of the Kargil War. Speaking about the current geopolitical uncertainty, Singh said, the consensus of yesterday on international norms have been broken, and countries are rearming themselves and spending more. India is trying to ensure that it becomes self-reliant in defence. But it also needs to ensure that its supply chains are in friendly countries and trusted geographies.  “Defence preparedness cannot depend upon fragile or overly concentrated supply chains.” India’s intention is to build up its defence-industrial base, Singh said.  Today, there are some 840 large and medium-sized companies with industrial licenses, and 17,000 small companies and startups in the defence sector. Domestic sales are worth Rs 1.78 trillion, and defence exports are at a record of about Rs 38,000 crore. “Our intention is to codevelop, coproduce and co-own many of our defence technologies with friendly foreign countries, (and) integrate Indian suppliers into global supply chains,” Singh said. India has become a top supplier of defence items such as ammunition to Europe mainly because of the “rearm Europe initiative”. Indian arms makers have sent at least $872 million worth of ammunition (including artillery and mortar shells) to European countries since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Most have been imported by 13 countries in eastern and central Europe, according to a recent Bloomberg report that cited the Trade Data Monitor’s sourcing of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry data. Before that India exported such items worth more than $49 million.   India and the European Union announced their first comprehensive security and defence partnership alongside concluding negotiations for a free-trade agreement in January. France is a leading supplier of up-end defence goods to India. The country’s bilateral defence ties also extend to West Asia and Africa.

item.title: Sebi mulls automatic approval for investments, activities by exchanges
item.description: Sebi has proposed an automatic approval route for certain activities and investments by market infrastructure institutions, subject to financial limits and governance safeguards.
item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / News / Sebi mulls automatic approval for investments, activities by exchanges

Sebi mulls automatic approval for investments, activities by exchanges Sebi has proposed an automatic approval route for certain activities and investments by market infrastructure institutions, subject to financial limits and governance safeguards.

Sebi has proposed allowing stock exchanges and depositories to undertake certain activities and investments without prior regulatory approval, subject to safeguards. (Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 11:45 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Markets regulator Sebi has proposed allowing stock and depositories to deploy funds and undertake activities related to their core functions without its prior approval, a move aimed at reducing regulatory burden and improving ease of doing business.   In its consultation paper, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has proposed an automatic approval route for activities related or incidental to the core functions of exchanges and depositories, subject to specified financial limits and governance safeguards.   The proposal covers market infrastructure institutions (MIIs), which currently require prior Sebi approval for activities involving fund deployment or otherwise, except for treasury investments made under a board-approved investment policy.

"The MIIs (excluding the recognized clearing corporations) may engage in activities whether involving deployment of funds or otherwise, without prior approval of Sebi (herein after referred to as the "automatic route"), in the following routes (A&B) and subject to the financial limits ... and the governance conditions," Sebi said.   Under the proposed framework, the automatic Route A would cover activities undertaken pursuant to Sebi directions, certain transfers of shares within an MII group, and deployment of funds by an operating subsidiary exclusively from its own operational earnings. Also Read

Sebi orders Avadhut Sathe Trading Academy and its founder to refund ₹546 cr

Sebi eases call-recording mandate for research analysts dealing with funds

Whistleblower tipoffs on insider trading up sharply as Sebi gets 25 in FY26 premium

Sebi warns investors against fraudulent WhatsApp stock tip groups

Sebi allows margin relief on subsequent trades against early pay-in

The Route B would cover activities similar in function to those carried out by an MII through an entity regulated by another financial sector regulator in India, provided Sebi has previously approved such activity and its nature remains unchanged.

Also, Sebi has proposed capping aggregate fund deployment under the automatic route in a financial year at the lower of 5 per cent of the MII's net worth as of March 31 of the preceding financial year or the regulatory minimum net worth requirement. Further, the MII's net worth after the proposed deployment should not fall below 1.5 times the minimum net worth prescribed by the regulator.   The proposed framework also mandates governance safeguards, including prior approval of each new activity or fund deployment by the MII's governing board, measures to prevent conflicts of interest, and compliance with fit-and-proper criteria by investee companies, their directors and shareholders.

MIIs would also be required to put in place board-approved standard operating procedures and submit half-yearly reports to   Sebi detailing activities undertaken under the automatic route within 30 days of the end of each half-year.   The regulator said the existing framework imposes the same approval requirement on activities irrespective of their size, nature or risk, creating an additional compliance burden even for small investments that directly support market operations.   It also noted that separate approvals could lead to duplication of regulatory scrutiny in cases where activities are already directed by Sebi or involve entities regulated by other financial sector regulators.   The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has sought public comments till November 12 on the proposals.

item.content:encoded:
Home / Companies / News / Apple India revenue grows 32% to cross ₹1 trillion mark in FY26: Tofler

Apple India revenue grows 32% to cross ₹1 trillion mark in FY26: Tofler The company's total expenses for the fiscal were reported at Rs 96,224 crore, Tofler said

(Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India New Delhi 1 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 11:17 PM IST

Listen to This Article

iPhone maker Apple's India revenue grew by over 32 per cent to Rs 1,04,607 crore in FY26, according to the document shared by market intelligence firm Tofler. The company recorded revenue of Rs 79,060.5 crore in FY25. "Apple India Private Limited provides and markets Apple brand products and software, and reported its revenues for the financial year 2025-26 at Rs 1,04,607 crore, a 32 per cent jump since the last financial year," Tofler said. Apple India net profit grew by 66 per cent to Rs 5,311 crore in the same fiscal. The company's total expenses for the fiscal were reported at Rs 96,224 crore, Tofler said.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
